pages.x: Gaul, roughly today's France and Belgium, was a land of Celtic peoples, with hill towns, gold coins and druid priests, split into dozens of rival tribes. Rome already held the south coast. In 58 BC its governor, Julius Caesar, deep in debt and hungry for glory, found reasons to march in.

In his first summer Caesar stopped the Helvetii, a whole people on the move with their wagons from what is now Switzerland, near Bibracte. Then he drove a German king, Ariovistus, back over the Rhine. Within three years most of Gaul had submitted.
In 55 BC Caesar's engineers bridged the Rhine in about ten days, driving wooden piles into the river bed at a slant against the current.
pages.fx: He crossed, burned villages for 18 days, came back and pulled the bridge down. It was a show of strength: Rome could go where it liked.

pages.x: He also crossed to Britain, twice, in 55 and 54 BC, the first Roman army to go there. Storms wrecked his ships, and the Britons fought from chariots, which the Romans had not faced for generations. He took hostages and promises of tribute, and left.

In 52 BC the Gauls rose together under a young noble of the Arverni, Vercingetorix. He had towns and farms burned so that the Romans could find no food, and beat Caesar at Gergovia, the worst defeat Caesar himself suffered in Gaul.

Vercingetorix shut himself up in the hill town of Alesia with 80,000 men. Caesar surrounded it with 16 km of walls and towers, then built a second ring of 21 km facing outwards against a huge Gaulish army coming to the rescue. Attacked from both sides at once, the Romans held.

Plutarch tells how Vercingetorix rode out of Alesia in his finest armour, circled Caesar on his horse, then jumped down and threw his weapons at Caesar's feet. He was kept in prison in Rome for six years, paraded in Caesar's triumph, and then strangled.

pages.x: Plutarch wrote that Caesar fought three million men, killed a million and enslaved a million more. The numbers are surely too high, but whole peoples were sold as slaves, and the trade made Caesar rich.

Caesar sent home reports each year, later published as The Gallic War. Written about himself as "Caesar", in plain, clear Latin, it opens: all Gaul is divided into three parts. It was propaganda, but it is also our main source, and for centuries pupils learned Latin from it.

The conquest made Caesar rich, famous and strong enough to take Rome itself. Gaul stayed Roman for 500 years: its people came to speak Latin, which grew into French, and Roman towns grew into cities such as Lyon and Paris.
